title: Reservoir Computing Foundations
intro: Reservoir computing trains only a linear readout on the states of a fixed, driven dynamical system; everything quantum reservoir computing does is this recipe with a quantum system as the reservoir. This topic sets out the classical theory that the quantum pages lean on: echo state networks, the echo state property, memory and processing capacity, physical reservoirs and the benchmark tasks.

blocks.text: The recipe in one equation pair
A reservoir is a driven dynamical system with state $x_k$, fed an input sequence $u_k$ one step at a time. Only the readout is learned:

blocks.caption: The reservoir map $F$ is fixed (random, or set by physics). Only $W_{\mathrm{out}}$ is trained.

blocks.text: Because $\hat y_k$ is linear in the trained weights, training is a least-squares problem with a closed-form solution: no backpropagation through time, no vanishing gradients, no local minima. The price is that the reservoir has to supply, by itself, the features a linear map needs: a fading trace of past inputs (memory) and nonlinear functions of them (processing). The whole field is about which systems $F$ supply good features, and how to read them out cheaply.

items: Fading memory, formalised as the echo state property: after a washout the state depends only on the recent inputs, not on the initial state. Without it the same input gives different outputs on different runs, and the readout cannot generalise.

Richness (separation): different input histories must map to linearly distinguishable states, and the state must contain nonlinear functions of the inputs. The information processing capacity counts this, and is bounded by the number of linearly independent state variables you read.

A readable state: you must be able to measure enough of $x_k$, with enough precision, at the rate the inputs arrive. For physical reservoirs this is often the binding constraint, and for quantum reservoirs it is the central one, because a quantum state can only be read through repeated measurements.

blocks.text: What changes when the reservoir is quantum

In quantum reservoir computing the state is a density matrix $\rho_k$ of $n$ qubits, the map is a completely positive trace-preserving channel $\rho_k = \mathcal{T}_{u_k}(\rho_{k-1})$, and the features are expectation values $x_k^{(i)} = \operatorname{Tr}(O_i \rho_k)$. Each classical idea on this topic has a quantum counterpart:

items: Echo state property becomes contractivity of the input-driven channel: a unitary alone never forgets, so a quantum reservoir needs dissipation (a reset, a measurement or coupling to an environment).
The number of reservoir units $N$ becomes the number of independent observables you read, which can in principle reach $4^n-1$ for $n$ qubits, but each costs measurement shots.
Virtual nodes from delay-line photonics reappear as sampling the quantum system several times between inputs.
Benchmarks (short-term memory, NARMA, parity, Mackey-Glass) are the same, so classical baselines are directly comparable.
$u_k$ or $s_k$: the scalar input at step $k$ (quantum pages use $s_k \in [0,1]$ because it sets a qubit amplitude).
$x_k \in \mathbb{R}^N$: the feature vector read at step $k$ (reservoir state for an ESN, expectation values for a quantum reservoir).
$y_k$: target, $\hat y_k$: readout prediction; washout, train and test windows are consecutive blocks of one input stream.
$\mathrm{MC}$: linear memory capacity; $C_{\mathrm{tot}}$: total information processing capacity; NMSE: mean squared error divided by the target variance.
Echo State Networks (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-networks): the canonical reservoir, its update rule, hyperparameters and ridge-regression readout.
The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property): when a driven system forgets its initial state, the sufficient and necessary conditions, and the role of the input.

Memory and Processing Capacity (#/qrc/foundations/memory-and-capacity): the linear memory function, the bound $\mathrm{MC} \le N$, information processing capacity and the memory-nonlinearity trade-off.
Physical Reservoirs (#/qrc/foundations/physical-reservoirs): computing with buckets, lasers, spin oscillators and soft bodies; delay lines and virtual nodes.
Benchmark Tasks and Evaluation (#/qrc/foundations/benchmark-tasks): the tasks QRC papers report, how to evaluate fairly, and the baselines to beat.

blocks.text: If you already know ESNs well, read the echo state property and capacity pages anyway: the quantum pages use the contraction picture and the capacity bound constantly.
